title: Relational Database Internals
summary: Open the magic SQL box and it's just four tricks: pages in RAM, B+tree indexes, a log for crash safety, and version chains for concurrency.

blocks.markdown:
A relational database is a few clever tricks stacked together to give fast lookups plus crash-safe transactions.

- A table is a pile of fixed-size **pages** (8 or 16 KB) on disk; the DB reads whole pages, never single rows.
- Hot pages live in RAM in the **buffer pool**; most tuning is about keeping the right pages there.
- A **B+tree index** turns "scan a million rows" into "follow 3-4 pointers."
- A **transaction** is all-or-nothing work; the **write-ahead log** makes it survive crashes.

blocks.subTitle: Which trick for which job
blocks.markdown:
Pick the mechanism that fits the access pattern.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Point lookup by key | B+tree index |
| Scanning most of the table | Full scan, no index |
| Reads must never block | MVCC database |
| Joining big unsorted tables | Hash join |

blocks.subTitle: Pages and the buffer pool
blocks.markdown:
The DB moves data in whole **pages**, and caches the hot ones in RAM.

- A page holds a header plus dozens to a couple hundred rows; oversized values spill to overflow pages.
- The **buffer pool** is RAM (often 60-80% of the box) caching pages. A **hit** serves from RAM in sub-microseconds; a **miss** reads disk and evicts an LRU victim.
- Modifying a cached page makes it **dirty**; dirty pages flush to disk later in batches, not on every change.
- Watch the **hit ratio** — a drop from 99.9% to 95% can spike disk I/O 50x.

blocks.subTitle: B+tree indexes
blocks.markdown:
An index is a sorted side-structure that gives O(log n) lookups instead of a full scan.

![B+tree lookup walking from root to leaf for key 72](assets/relational-db-internals/btree-lookup.svg)

- Internal nodes are **signposts** (key ranges and child pointers); leaves hold sorted keys plus the row or a pointer to it.
- High **fan-out** (~400 keys per page) keeps it shallow: 4 levels reach 25 billion rows, so a lookup touches only **3-4 pages**.
- Leaves are linked, so once you find a range start you walk sideways — fast `BETWEEN` scans.

assets.alt: B+tree lookup walking from root to leaf for key 72

blocks.subTitle: Clustered vs secondary index
blocks.markdown:
A clustered index *is* the table; a secondary index points back to it.

- **Clustered** — full rows live in the leaves in key order. InnoDB clusters on the primary key, so a PK lookup lands on the row in one walk. One per table.
- **Secondary** — a separate tree whose leaves hold the column plus a row reference; reading other columns needs a second **bookmark lookup**.
- A **covering index** includes every column the query needs, so it never touches the table.
- Postgres differs: tables are unordered **heaps** and all indexes are secondary.

blocks.subTitle: Transactions and ACID
blocks.markdown:
A transaction is work bracketed by `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` that the DB promises four things about.

- **Atomicity** — all-or-nothing; a rollback looks as if nothing ran.
- **Consistency** — moves from one valid state to another, respecting constraints.
- **Isolation** — concurrent transactions don't step on each other.
- **Durability** — once `COMMIT` returns, the data survives a crash.

Atomicity and durability are the WAL's job; isolation is MVCC and locking's job.

blocks.subTitle: Isolation levels & anomalies
blocks.markdown:
Higher isolation blocks more anomalies but costs more concurrency.

- **Dirty read** — reading another transaction's uncommitted change.
- **Non-repeatable read** — re-reading a row and getting a different committed value.
- **Phantom** — re-running a range query and seeing new committed rows.

Levels, weakest to strongest: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED (stops dirty), REPEATABLE READ (stops non-repeatable), SERIALIZABLE (stops all plus write skew). Note: InnoDB and Postgres block most phantoms at REPEATABLE READ, stronger than the standard.

blocks.subTitle: MVCC
blocks.markdown:
MVCC keeps multiple versions of each row so readers and writers never block each other.

![MVCC version chain with three snapshots reading different committed versions](assets/relational-db-internals/mvcc-version-chain.svg)

- An update writes a **new version** tagged with the transaction id instead of overwriting; versions form a chain.
- A reader uses its **snapshot** to return the newest version committed before it started.
- Cost is **bloat**: dead versions pile up. Postgres reclaims them with **VACUUM**; InnoDB purges its **undo log**.

assets.alt: MVCC version chain with three snapshots reading different committed versions

blocks.subTitle: The write-ahead log
blocks.markdown:
One rule gives durability and atomicity: write the log record before the data.

![WAL write path: modify page, append to log, fsync, commit, flush pages later](assets/relational-db-internals/wal-write-path.svg)

- The change hits the buffer pool and a compact record is appended to the **WAL**; on `COMMIT` the WAL is **fsync'd**, then commit is acked.
- Dirty data pages flush later at a **checkpoint** — durability comes from the log, not the data files.
- Fast because it's one **sequential** append, not many random writes. **Group commit** batches fsyncs.
- On recovery: **redo** committed changes since the last checkpoint, then **undo** in-flight ones.

assets.alt: WAL write path: modify page, append to log, fsync, commit, flush pages later

blocks.subTitle: Joins & query planning
blocks.markdown:
SQL is declarative: you say *what*, the cost-based planner decides *how*, using table statistics.

Three join algorithms the planner chooses between:
- **Nested loop** — for each outer row, probe the inner; great when outer is small and inner is indexed.
- **Hash join** — build a hash table on the smaller input, probe with the larger; best for two big unindexed tables.
- **Merge join** — sort both by the key and walk together; cheap when inputs are already sorted.

Stale statistics cause sudden bad plans; inspect choices with `EXPLAIN`.

blocks.subTitle: The recurring tensions
blocks.markdown:
Every knob trades one cost for another.

| Tension | The trade |
|---|---|
| Indexes | Faster reads, slower writes |
| Isolation | More safety, less concurrency |
| fsync | More durability, higher latency |
| Buffer pool | Higher hit ratio, less free RAM |

Use the lowest isolation that's correct, index only hot selective paths, and relax fsync only when a sub-second loss window is acceptable.

blocks.subTitle: Real engines & signals
blocks.markdown:
The same internals show up differently across engines and dashboards.

- **Postgres** — heap tables, all-secondary indexes, inline versions cleaned by autovacuum; SERIALIZABLE via SSI ([consistency-replication](consistency-replication)).
- **MySQL/InnoDB** — clustered on PK, old versions in an undo log, REPEATABLE READ with next-key locks.
- **Watch:** sawtooth p99 on commit (checkpoint storms), rising replication lag, long idle-in-transaction sessions pinning VACUUM, and full-scan spikes from stale stats.

The myths that bite in interviews and production:

- **"An index always helps."** For a query matching most of the table, a sequential scan beats index plus bookmark lookups.
- **"MVCC means no locks."** Two writers to the same row still serialize via exclusive locks and can deadlock.
- **"COMMIT writes the data files."** It flushes the WAL; pages flush later at a checkpoint.
- **"VACUUM is optional."** Dead tuples bloat tables and risk transaction-id wraparound.
- **Random UUID primary keys** scatter inserts in a clustered tree — use a monotonic key instead.
